contract_plain_english: For a real random variable and a tail exponent alpha, formulate and prove a quantitative characterization of the class with tails no heavier than exp(-c t^alpha). The characterization should be a genuine analogue of Proposition 2.7.1, relating suitable tail, moment, and exponential-integrability conditions and recovering the named alpha = 2 sub-gaussian and alpha = 1 sub-exponential cases. Because the exercise deliberately asks for 'a version,' it does not uniquely fix the alpha range, parameter normalization, constant dependence, exact property list, or a generalized centered-MGF clause.

source_evidence.observation: The exercise considers, more generally, distributions whose tail decay is of type exp(-c t^alpha) or faster.
The source identifies alpha = 2 with sub-gaussian distributions and alpha = 1 with sub-exponential distributions.
The requested task is to state and prove a version of Proposition 2.7.1 for such distributions.
The referenced proposition characterizes sub-exponential random variables by equivalent tail, moment, MGF-of-absolute-value, and one-point exponential-integrability properties.
Its quantitative equivalence means that one absolute constant C transfers any property i to any property j among properties 1, 2, 3, and 4 with K_j at most C K_i.
For a centered random variable, the referenced proposition additionally includes a local quadratic MGF condition for X itself.

binders: A real-valued random variable X (Proposition 2.7.1 and Exercise 2.7.3, PDF pages 20-22; printed pages 31-33).
A tail exponent alpha governing decay of type exp(-c t^alpha) (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).
Positive scale parameters for whichever analogue properties are stated, in the quantitative style of Proposition 2.7.1 (Proposition 2.7.1 and footnote 7, PDF page 20; printed page 31).
conclusions: State a mathematically precise version of Proposition 2.7.1 that characterizes distributions with tail decay of type exp(-c t^alpha) or faster (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).
Prove the stated characterization, rather than merely naming or defining the generalized class (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).
The formulation must be compatible with the source's identifications alpha = 2 as sub-gaussian and alpha = 1 as sub-exponential (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).

As a version of Proposition 2.7.1, the result must express quantitative relationships among appropriate tail, moment, and exponential-integrability formulations, while the source leaves the exact list and normalization to the solver (Proposition 2.7.1, PDF pages 20-22, printed pages 31-33; Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22, printed page 33).
definitions_and_conventions: In Proposition 2.7.1(a), the sub-exponential tail form is P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t/K_1) for every t >= 0 (PDF page 21; printed page 32).
In Proposition 2.7.1(b), the moment form is ||X||_{L^p} <= K_2 p for every p >= 1 (PDF page 21; printed page 32).
In Proposition 2.7.1(c)-(d), the exponential-integrability forms are an interval MGF bound for |X| and the one-point bound E exp(|X|/K_4) <= 2 (PDF page 21; printed page 32).

The precise comparison convention for Proposition 2.7.1(a)-(d) uses one absolute C such that property i with K_i implies property j with K_j <= C K_i for every i,j in {1,2,3,4} (footnote 7, PDF page 20; printed page 31).
When E X = 0, Proposition 2.7.1(e) is a local quadratic MGF bound for X and is also equivalent to (a)-(d) in the alpha = 1 sub-exponential setting (PDF page 21; printed page 32).
hypotheses: X belongs to the class whose tails decay like exp(-c t^alpha) or faster (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).

The exponent is to be in a regime where exp(-c t^alpha) expresses tail decay; the source exemplifies alpha = 2 and alpha = 1 but does not explicitly state its full range (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).
implicit_context: Probabilities, expectations, moments, and MGFs are taken for the random variable X under its underlying probability law (Proposition 2.7.1, PDF pages 20-22; printed pages 31-33).

The requested result is a generalization exercise, not a uniquely dictated verbatim theorem: the source says to state and prove 'a version' of Proposition 2.7.1 (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).

The answer must state and prove a version of Proposition 2.7.1; a definition alone or an unproved assertion does not satisfy the exercise (Exercise 2.7.3, PDF page 22; printed page 33).

The result must retain a quantitative comparison appropriate to the parameterized equivalence being generalized, since Proposition 2.7.1 explicitly compares its parameters by a constant factor (Proposition 2.7.1 statement and footnote 7, PDF page 20; printed page 31).
